1:
Why the boundaries are given at all draws answers that differ in figure rather than substance. puritan-evangelical Henry says God directs Moses to settle the line not as a geographer draws a map, merely to please the curious, but as a prince draws a grant, so that it may be certainly known what passes and is conveyed by it. reformed Calvin uses a domestic image for the same thing: God here undertakes the office of a prudent and careful father of a family, fixing the boundaries on every side so that their right to possess the land should never be called in question. Gill puts it practically, and adds on the next verse that the command is not to fix the borders, since God himself has determined the bounds of men’s habitations, but to take notice of the limits already fixed, so that they might know how far to go, whom to dispossess, what to divide, and how to preserve their right from the encroachments of neighbours. wesleyan-arminian Wesley adds a restraint: the limits are described to bound them in their wars and conquests, that they might not seek the enlargement of their empire after the manner of other nations, but be contented with their own portion.

Two of them measure the grant against a larger promise. Henry observes that a much greater possession had been promised, reaching to the Euphrates, which in due time they would have held had they been obedient — and so far the dominion of Israel did in fact extend under David and Solomon — whereas what is described here is Canaan only, the lot of the nine tribes and a half, the other two and a half being already settled. Wesley says the same and then measures the smaller thing: Canaan proper lay in a very little compass, about a hundred and fifty miles in length and fifty in breadth, and this was the one spot of ground in which for many ages God was known. Its littleness, he adds, was abundantly compensated by its fruitfulness, since otherwise it could not have sustained so numerous a nation — and he draws the moral, that God often gives his own people a very small share of the world, but those whose portion is in heaven can be content with a small pittance of this earth. Henry makes the point differently: the land was limited within certain bounds because God appoints the bounds of our habitation.

Calvin traces the southern line himself, beginning at that quarter and noting that the district of Bashan and everything the Israelites had won before crossing the Jordan is included, so that the addition had God’s approval; he carries the line as far as the wilderness of Zin and the borders of Edom, round from Kadesh-barnea by Addar and the passage of Azmon to the stream at the end. On what that stream is he reports a long dispute among commentators and sides with the modern conclusion that the river of Egypt, when named as a boundary, cannot be the Nile. grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the southern boundary here is identical with the line given in Joshua for the territory of Judah, and take the general description first — the south side reaching from the desert of Zin along the sides of Edom — distinguishing the Hebrew idiom used here, which denotes contact along a long stretch, from the similar phrase used of contact at a single point.

wesleyan-arminian Clarke, having opened with an outline of the whole chapter, declines the topography altogether: all description here, he says, is useless, and the situation and boundaries of the land of Canaan can only be known by an actual survey or by consulting a good map.
3:
The southern line is traced from the Dead Sea westward. reformed Gill notes that this border ran from east to west, and that the verb rendered fetch a compass means it did not go on in a straight line but turned about. wesleyan-arminian Wesley describes the whole quarter as running from east to west by many windings and turnings, forced on it by the mountains and rivers, and explains the name of the salt sea from the salt and sulphurous taste of its waters, the border meeting it at its eastern part where the eastern and southern lines join. grammatical-historical Ellicott would render the opening more exactly — the border shall turn on the south side of the ascent of Akrabbim and pass over to Zin, its goings forth being on the south of Kadesh-barnea — and takes the line to run south-westerly from the southern tongue of the Dead Sea to that ascent, then westward to Kadesh-barnea, which lay at the western extremity of the desert of Zin and was included within the territory. The height of Akrabbim he identifies with a row of white cliffs running obliquely across the Arabah about eight miles from the Dead Sea.

Ellicott admits that the exact site of some of these places has never been positively ascertained, but holds there is little doubt the line followed the valleys that form a natural division between the cultivated land and the desert, from the Arabah on the east to the Mediterranean on the west. Keil and Delitzsch, whose comment runs on into the next section, add that the western boundary was to be the great sea together with its territory, that is, the Mediterranean and its coast. Clarke identifies the salt sea plainly as the Dead Sea.

The one real disagreement concerns the stream at the western end of the southern line. Clarke reports two identifications, the eastern branch of the Nile, or else a river lying south of the land of the Philistines and falling into the bay. Wesley takes it for the watercourse called Sihor, which divided Egypt from Canaan, and adds a note on the closing word: the sea here means the midland sea, called the sea by way of eminence, whereas the other so-called seas of that country are in truth only lakes. Ellicott names it outright as the Wady-el-Arish, and makes it the western boundary until it reached the sea. Wesley also places Azmon at the west end of the mount of Edom, and reads the phrase rendered from the south as meaning rather onward toward the south.
6:
The western border needs no tracing, and the witnesses use the space for philology. wesleyan-arminian Clarke explains why the Mediterranean is called the great sea: it is so named to distinguish it from the Dead Sea, the sea of Tiberias and the rest, which are only a sort of lakes. In Hebrew, he adds, there is properly but one term, applied to all collections of water apparently stagnant and generally rendered sea, and the Greek of the New Testament follows the Hebrew in using one word whether it speaks of the Mediterranean or of the lake of Galilee. grammatical-historical Ellicott would render the clause more exactly, that they shall have the great sea and its border, meaning its coast. Wesley marks how much of that sea is in view: the midland sea from south to north, so far as it runs parallel with mount Libanus. reformed Gill notes only that this is the western border of the land of Canaan.

The northern line is another matter. Keil and Delitzsch say flatly that it cannot be determined with certainty: of all the places named, Hamath — the modern Hamah, the Epiphania of the Greeks and Romans on the Orontes — is the only one whose situation is well known, and the standing geographical phrase for the northern limit of Israel is so indefinite that the line cannot be fixed exactly. Ellicott takes up the hardest point, which mountain is meant by Hor. Some have thought it Hermon, but he quotes the objection that Hermon stands too far eastward to answer the conditions of the problem, its author preferring some peak very near the Mediterranean; and he reports another opinion that it was probably one of the peaks belonging to the Lebanon range and discernible from Sidon. Wesley rules out one identification and settles on another: it is not the Hor where Aaron died, which lay southward and bordered on Edom, but another mountain, conceived to be Libanus, which is elsewhere named as the northern border, and which different peoples called by different names — here Hor, which simply means a mountain, by way of eminence.

The remaining places are pursued with less confidence still. Gill takes the entrance of Hamath to be a narrow pass leading from the land of Canaan into Syria, through the valley lying between Lebanon and Antilibanus, and reports the older identification of Hamath with Antioch before preferring Epiphania. On Ziphron he notes that one Targum calls it Zapherin, and that an early father says the city was in his own day called Zephyrium, a town in Cilicia — which Gill thinks lies at too great a distance to be right. Ellicott agrees that both Ziphron and the village of Enan are unknown, and supposes only that the line probably crossed the northern portion of Lebanon.

Keil and Delitzsch, running on into the eastern side, follow the upper line from Hazar-enan to Shepham, whose site is unknown, and from Shepham down to Riblah on the east of Ain. The definite article and the careful phrase to the east of the fountain, they argue, show that this Riblah must be distinguished from the Riblah in the land of Hamath with which it is generally identified, and they take Ain for a great fountain at the foot of the range.
10:
The eastern line is traced through places that are mostly guesswork. reformed Gill starts from where the northern border ended, a spot an early father says the Hebrews called Apamia, as both Targums do here, and places Shepham as a city between Hazar-enan and Riblah in the territory of Naphtali. On the descent that follows he passes on a rabbinic observation: when a border runs from north toward south it is said to go down. grammatical-historical Ellicott takes the fountain named here to be the great spring of Neba Anjar at the foot of Antilibanus, and argues that if so, this Riblah must be a different place from the Riblah in the land of Hamath which appears in the later histories. From that point the boundary ran southward along the side — the Hebrew says the shoulder — of the lake of Chinnereth, and from there the eastern limit was the Jordan itself down to the Dead Sea. Keil and Delitzsch, whose comment overruns into the next section, note that the land so bounded was to be distributed by lot to the nine tribes and a half, the others having already received their portion beyond the river.

Gill knows the rival identification and rejects it. Riblah, he reports, is said to lie in the land of Hamath, which an early father took for Antioch of Syria, while both Targums understand by it Daphne in the suburbs of Antioch — but this, he says, seems to be carrying the limits of the land too far. On the lake, Ellicott notes that Chinnereth appears to have been the name of a district as well as of a town, and that the name is supposed to derive from the word for a harp; in later times the city was called Genusar, whence the form found in the Gospels. wesleyan-arminian Clarke simply lists the equivalents, that the sea of Chinnereth is the same as the sea of Galilee, of Tiberias and of Gennesareth.

The last river gets more attention than the rest of the border together. Gill calls the Jordan a well-known river east of the land; Clarke calls it famous in both Testaments and traces its course from the foot of Mount Libanus through the sea of Chinnereth into the Dead Sea, from which it has no outlet. He then lists what was done in it and by it: God cut off its waters as he had the Red Sea, so that they stood in a heap on either side and the people passed over dry ground; Elijah and Elisha each divided it; the Syrian general was cured of his leprosy by washing in it at the prophet’s word; John baptized great multitudes of the people in it; and in it Christ himself was baptized, the Spirit descending on him and the voice from heaven proclaiming him.
13:
The land having been bounded, it is now assigned. grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch state the arrangement plainly: the land within the boundaries just described was to be distributed by lot among the nine tribes and a half, since Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh had already received their inheritance on the other side of the Jordan. reformed Gill notes only that Moses strictly enjoins them to observe what he is about to say, and identifies the tribes concerned. Ellicott corrects the familiar rendering of the last clause: rather than on this side Jordan, the sense is along the side or bank of the river.

reformed Calvin takes up the question the arrangement raises. Though the statement repeats what has been said before, it is not superfluous, since it sets the new allotment of the nine tribes and a half against the grant already made of the district of Bashan. The exception for the lands beyond Jordan, he insists, does not shut Reuben and Gad and the half tribe out of their part of the promised inheritance as though they were disinherited and banished beyond the boundaries God had prescribed; it excludes them only from the casting of lots, because by a special privilege obtained from their brethren they already held what would otherwise have fallen within the common inheritance. Nor had this been revealed from the beginning: God in his indulgence complied with their request, and by that compliance the boundaries of the land were enlarged. It would have been absurd, Calvin adds, that no place at all should be given them among their brethren in the land of promise.

wesleyan-arminian Clarke stops over the word inherit and finds much of what is said about this land peculiarly emphatic, since it holds a multitude of advantages in climate, soil and situation. It is bounded on the south by a ridge of mountains that separates it from Arabia and screens it from the burning and often pestiferous winds blowing off the desert; on the west by the Mediterranean; on the north by Mount Libanus, which defends it from the cold northern blasts; and on the east by the Jordan with its fertile, well-watered plains. He then quotes the description God himself gave of it — a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths springing out of valleys and hills, a land of wheat and barley and vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey, where there was no scarcity of bread and where iron and copper mines abounded — and calls it finely diversified with hills and valleys and well watered throughout.
16:
puritan-evangelical Henry notices what is taken for granted. God appoints commissioners for dividing the land though as yet not a stroke had been struck toward conquering it, and names no generals to carry on the war, because the land was to be got not by their own sword or bow but by the power and favour of God. So confident were they to be of victory while God fought for them that the men are named now who would be entrusted with the division, presiding at the lots, settling any controversy, and seeing that all was done fairly. Henry adds a figure: the principal commissioners, Eleazar and Joshua, typify Christ, who as priest and king divides the heavenly Canaan among the spiritual Israel; and yet, as they were to proceed by lot, so Christ acknowledges that the disposal must rest with the Father’s will. reformed Gill says the appointment was made at the same time as the boundaries, so that the division might be done in the most impartial manner and to the satisfaction of all.

The obvious objection is Calvin’s. If the Israelites were to divide the land among themselves by lot, why was the authority of judges required at all, as though anything were left for them to decide? His answer turns on the fact that the distribution had to take account of the numbers in each tribe, so that two things were needed: that God should show by his own decree which district fell to which tribe, and that the dimensions should be proportionate to the occupants. The lot was still necessary, since many would have been averse to the sea-coast, or preferred the centre to the extremities, or refused to be banished to the mountains, and would have contended beyond measure in murmurings and strife; so the lot placed each tribe where God pleased, although the judges, with the high priest and Joshua, had beforehand divided the land into ten portions. grammatical-historical Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the other end: the position of the territory only, and not its dimensions, was determined by lot, and the presence of the princes gave security for the equity and impartiality of the whole.

Who the commissioners were is set out carefully. Ellicott notes that besides Eleazar the high priest and Joshua the commander of the army, one chief man was to be taken from each of the ten tribes interested in the division, as one from each tribe had been associated with Moses and Aaron at the first census; and that apart from Caleb none of these princes is named anywhere else. Keil and Delitzsch make the same count and add a distinction, that these were heads of fathers’ houses within the tribes rather than heads of tribes. Gill explains the arithmetic — ten princes from the nine tribes and the half, none from Reuben and Gad because their inheritance lay elsewhere and none from Levi because that tribe was to have none in the land — and describes the men as of honour and probity, concerned for the good of their own tribes, who would see that no fraudulent method was used in the drawing.

Two points of rendering close the section. Gill reports that the phrase for dividing may be turned inherit the land for you, a rabbi taking it to mean the princes were to possess it in their tribes’ stead before distributing it — though whatever may be said for the princes, the same cannot be said of the two named first. Ellicott would render it which shall allot the land as an inheritance unto you. wesleyan-arminian Wesley describes the office of the first of them: Eleazar was to act in God’s name, to cast the lots, to prevent contentions, to consult God in cases of difficulty, and to transact the whole business in a solemn and religious manner.
19:
The list that follows is not in any of the orders used before, and two witnesses stop to say so. wesleyan-arminian Clarke calls it worthy of remark that Moses follows none of the arrangements of the tribes he had used at either muster or at the offerings of the princes, but sets them here exactly in the order in which they came to possess the land. Wesley notes the same difference from the earlier lists and draws his conclusion from it: the order is conformed to the several inheritances that afterwards fell to them by lot, which is to him an evident demonstration both of the infinite wisdom of God’s providence and of his peculiar care over his own people.

Clarke then walks the list down the map. Judah stands first, having the first lot, and dwelt in the south part of the land; Simeon comes next to him, because his inheritance lay inside the inheritance of the children of Judah; Benjamin is third, holding his portion beside Judah, between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph; Dan is fourth, his lot falling westward of Benjamin’s in the country of the Philistines. Fifth comes Manasseh, and sixth, beside him, his brother Ephraim, their inheritances lying behind that of Benjamin; and after these follow Zebulun, Issachar, Asher and Naphtali. The sequence is thus a map before it is a roll, and every name stands where its territory would afterwards stand, the southern tribes first and the northern last.

reformed Gill adds the one thing the list does not say of itself, and it bears on the whole appointment. The names were not left to the tribes to choose. They were nominated by the Lord himself, who best knew the capacities and the qualifications of each man for this particular service; so that the impartiality of the division was secured not only by the casting of the lot and by the standing of the men, but by the hand that had picked them in the first place. The first of them, Caleb, is the one name in the list that the later history makes familiar.
29: reformed Gill takes the closing formula for more than a summary of the list. The Lord did not merely name and appoint these men; he laid his commands upon them, and by that charge obliged them to the work. Gill also marks how early the order stands: it was made before the land had been conquered at all, and indeed before a single blow had been struck for it, which shows how sure and certain the possession already was to them. And it was carried out as given, the division being made at Shiloh, before the Lord, at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation — that is, in the presence of God himself, and in the most impartial and the most solemn manner that could well have been devised for such a business.
